description: Team of one. IT engineer working with Linux, cloud and Python. For this challenge I use NASA POWER data to measure and statistically test 45 years of temperature and precipitation trends for San Jose, CA, with a small tool anyone can rerun for any location.
summary: San Jose Trend Detective is a small, reproducible tool that checks whether a place's climate is really changing. It downloads 45 years (1981-2025) of NASA POWER monthly data for 2 m air temperature and precipitation, builds annual series, measures the trend per decade with least squares and tests it with the Mann-Kendall test. For San Jose, CA, temperature rose about +0.12 °C per decade (the last 10 years are ~0.5 °C warmer than the first 10), but the trend is not yet statistically significant (p = 0.22). Precipitation shows no trend but huge swings, from about 1,130 mm in 1983 (El Niño) to about 125 mm in 2013 (drought). The tool answers the challenge's questions: what changes, where (any latitude and longitude), how much, and whether it is significant. It runs with the Python standard library only.
details: What it does: for any latitude and longitude, the tool downloads monthly NASA POWER data (T2M, 2 m air temperature; PRECTOTCORR, precipitation) for 1981-2025, builds annual series (mean temperature, total precipitation), estimates the linear trend per decade with ordinary least squares, and tests significance with the Mann-Kendall trend test (z statistic and two-sided p-value at the 5 % level). It writes results.json and two SVG charts with the trend line. Benefits: it separates real trends from year-to-year noise, which is the core of the challenge. In San Jose, a chart that looks warmer is not yet a statistically significant trend over 45 years, and precipitation variability (El Niño 1983 against the 2013 drought) matters more than the average for water planning. Anyone can rerun it for their own location with one command. Tools: Python 3, standard library only (urllib, json, math), with no external packages. The demo is a 6-slide deck on GitHub Pages. Limitations: POWER is gridded reanalysis (~0.5°), so it is used for trends, not absolute values; the tests assume a monotonic trend and ignore autocorrelation. Next steps: heat-day counts from daily maximum temperature, several Bay Area grid cells side by side, and validation against NOAA station data.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) monthly point API: T2M and PRECTOTCORR
